title: Architecting the future: 5 Cloud Design Principles Every Beginner Should Know
description:
## Cloud architecture is not a simple deployment
When I initially began reading about cloud computing, I believed that it only revolved around spinning up virtual machines and putting files in buckets. However, as I started learning more and more, particularly during my preparation to take the AWS Solutions Architect certification, I came to realise something very important:

### Cloud does not only mean what you can deploy. It's about how you design it.

Whether your project is a simple blogging platform or a worldwide e-commerce platform, the architecture of your cloud deployment defines its reliability, scalability, security and economic efficiency. This is why the basics of cloud design are not only critical to passing exams but also to creating real-world working infrastructure.

## Design for Failure

Failure in the cloud is a reality, as the cloud is not foolproof. Hardware fails. Networks drop. Services glitch. The trick here is to come up with systems that handle failure gracefully.

### How to Apply It:

* Use more than one Availability Zone.
* Install disaster recovery and automated backups.
* Load balancing with Elastic Load Balancing will distribute the traffic on healthy instances.

### Example:

If you are hosting a blog on EC2, you need to deploy at least two instances across two AZs and use a load balancer. In that case, when one of the AZs fails, your site remains alive.

## Implement Elasticity

The ability to scale out or in, that is, to increase or decrease the capacity of the cloud according to the demand and elasticity, meaning your architecture can react dynamically without manual operations, is one of the largest advantages of the cloud.

### How to Apply It:

* Modify compute resources with Auto Scaling Groups.
* Use serverless compute (such as AWS Lambda and Fargate) when the workload is hard to predict.
* Select pay-as-you-go pricing systems to eliminate unnecessary over-provisioning.

### Example:

Black Friday may cause a surge in traffic to an online store. Under Auto Scaling, your EC2 instances would be automatically increased to meet the load and reduced later on to save money.

## Secure Your Architecture

Cloud security is a collective effort. AWS keeps the infrastructure secure, but you keep your applications, data and access controls secure.

### How to Apply It:

* Adhere to IAM best practice: employ roles, policies and least privilege.
* Secure data on the rest and on transit.
* Make sensitive accounts multi-factor authenticated (MFA).

### Example:

When you use S3 to store user data, you should enable encryption and use bucket policies and IAM roles, not public permissions, to restrict your access.

## Cost Optimization

The cloud charges you for what you use, but unless properly planned, expenses can run out of control. Cost optimisation refers to the creation of systems that are capable of producing value without wastage.

### How to Apply It:

* Calculate the AWS Pricing.
* Select appropriate types of instances and classes.
* Established budgets and alerts to check on expenditures.

### Example:

Rather than archiving files on the S3, move them to the S3 Glacier, which will be far cheaper and rarely used.

## Monitor and Improve

Architecture isn't static. You must have an insight into how your systems work so that you can repeat, refine and debug.

### How to Apply It:

* Metrics and alarms: Use Amazon CloudWatch.
* Trace requests and find bottlenecks with AWS X-Ray.
* Create a feedback loop so that the performance can continue to improve.

### Example:

When your application is becoming sluggish, CloudWatch metrics may indicate that you are consuming a lot of CPU. Then you can scale out or change the type of instance.

## Summary: Small is Big

These five principles apply to enterprise architects, but they also apply to anyone building in the cloud. Although you may only be installing a portfolio site or a demo application, the application of these concepts will make your solutions more sustainable and resistant to changes over time.

As I proceed in attaining my certified solutions architect, I am finding that good architecture is not about complexity but rather about clarity, stability, and intent.

So start small. Apply one principle. Then another. Before you know it, you'll be architecting the future.

title: From Curiousity to Certification: My Journey to Becoming an AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner
description:
## Introduction: Why I Chose the Cloud

Not long ago, sometime in January 2025, I was just another tech enthusiast trying to figure out where I fit in the vast world of IT. I’d heard of “cloud computing” and “cybersecurity” (big guys in my head), but they felt distant, like something reserved for ‘Silicon Valley’ engineers. Still, I couldn’t shake the feeling that the cloud was the future. And if I wanted to build solutions that scale, adapt, and matter, I needed to understand it.

So I made a decision to start the cloud journey with the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner. It was the perfect entry point with no deep coding required, just a solid grasp of cloud fundamentals. What began as curiosity quickly became an interest, mission and joy.

## My Study Strategy

I didn’t have a fancy bootcamp or a mentor guiding me; I wanted to start then and there. I had grit, though, Google, and a few golden resources:

* ALX AWS Cloud Computing Course: The almost-free cloud computing course started with a professional foundation drilling that helped to shape the direction and laid the path to taking a professional programme. The course was clear, structured, and engaging.

* YouTube Channels: Especially freeCodeCamp and Tech with Lucy. They helped break down concepts with visuals that stuck.

* ALX Cloud Computing Cohort: The experience was very dear and unique, and daily motivation and discussion kept the spark alive. Motivations, practice questions and answers were shared regularly.

* Practice Exams: I used the Kananinirav website, AWS Skill Builder and a couple of other websites to simulate the real test environment.

## Time Management

Managing time efficiently was a challenge, and it tested my ability as an industrial engineering student. I followed the weeks allocated by ALX for learning and gave myself 2 weeks to study and practise fervently for the exams; I studied almost 4 hours daily. I created flashcards and notes for key terms and reviewed them during idle moments.

## Key Concepts That Changed My Thinking

Here are three ideas that really stuck with me:

* Shared Responsibility Model: AWS secures the cloud infrastructure, but you secure what you put in it. It is essential to be aware of that distinction.

* Global Infrastructure: Understanding Regions, Availability Zones, and Edge Locations helped me visualise how AWS delivers speed and resilience worldwide.

* Pricing Models: Pay-as-you-go, Reserved Instances, and Spot Instances. Learning how billing works made me realise the cloud isn’t just technical and one-size-fits-all; it is specific and strategic.

## Exam Tips: What Helped Me Pass

* Don’t Memorise but Understand: The exam isn’t about regurgitating facts. It’s about applying concepts. For example, knowing why S3 is better for static websites than EC2.

* Watch for Tricky Wording: Some questions test your ability to distinguish between similar services (e.g., CloudTrail vs. CloudWatch).

* Use Elimination: Often, two options are clearly wrong. Narrow it down and trust your gut.

What surprised me most during my exam was how much the exam focuses on business value. It’s not just tech; it’s about how the cloud helps organisations innovate and save costs.

## What’s Next: Levelling Up to Solutions Architect

Passing the Cloud Practitioner exam gave me confidence not just in AWS, but in myself. Now, I’m preparing for the AWS Solutions Architect Associate certification. It’s more technical, more hands-on, and I'm gearing up for it.

I plan to document that journey too, sharing my study plan, projects, and lessons learned. Because if there’s one thing I’ve realised, it’s this: 

### The cloud isn’t just a career path. It’s a mindset of curiosity, adaptability, and building for the future.
